pairs.source_norm: was the triage safe to run under an embedding matcher as built
pairs.source_text: Was the triage safe to run under an embedding matcher as built?
pairs.target_text: No — cluster.py applied a character length-ratio prune (2*min/(la+lb) < bar) UNCONDITIONALLY as a cheap upper bound on difflib's ratio. That bound is real for difflib and false for cosine: a short paraphrase of a long question has a poor length ratio and a high semantic similarity, so the prune would have silently dropped exactly the re-worded edges the semantic matcher exists to find. pairs.source_norm: a verifier who already has an ed25519 private key from somewhere else a prior browser session on another device a keyring jsons private field being migrated to true client custody needs to bring it into this page what form does the import accept and why not offer both raw and pkcs8
pairs.source_text: A verifier who already has an Ed25519 private key from somewhere else — a prior browser session on another device, a keyring JSON's `private` field being migrated to true client custody — needs to bring it into this page. What form does the import accept, and why not offer both raw and PKCS8?
pairs.target_text: Raw 32-byte hex only — the exact form `nestor.keyring.VerifierKey`/`_ed25519_generate` already use (`Ed25519PrivateKey.private_bytes(Encoding.Raw, PrivateFormat.Raw, NoEncryption())`), so a key already living in a Nestor keyring file's `private` field pastes in unmodified. WebCrypto's `importKey` does not accept `"raw"` as a format for an Ed25519 PRIVATE key at all (measured: `Cannot create a key using the specified key usages` — raw import only works for the public half); the page works around this by prepending the fixed, parameter-free PKCS8 DER header for Ed25519 (`302e020100300506032b657004220420`, 16 bytes, constant because Ed25519 PKCS8 carries no algorithm parameters) to the pasted 32 bytes and importing THAT as `"pkcs8"` — verified byte-for-byte against a real `generateKey`+`exportKey("pkcs8")` round trip in the same Chromium build before relying on it. An optional public-hex field lets the page self-check the pair (sign a random client-side challenge with the imported private key, verify it against the imported public key, both via `crypto.subtle`, entirely client-side) before persisting — catching a copy-paste mismatch instead of silently persisting a key that will only fail at seal time.

pairs.source_norm: how does the browser get an ed25519 keypair and what extractable flag does the private half get
pairs.source_text: How does the browser get an Ed25519 keypair, and what extractable flag does the private half get?
pairs.target_text: Primary flow: `crypto.subtle.generateKey({name:"Ed25519"}, false, ["sign","verify"])` — extractable=false. WebCrypto applies that flag to the returned PRIVATE key only; the spec (and this Chromium build, measured directly: `privExtractable: false, pubExtractable: true`) always returns the public key with extractable=true regardless of the argument, which is exactly the asymmetry this page needs — the public half must leave the browser (to enroll), the private half must not be able to. The private CryptoKey is then stored, still non-extractable, as a structured-clone value directly in IndexedDB (a documented, standard use of IndexedDB for unexportable key material) keyed by verifier name; `crypto.subtle.exportKey("raw", publicKey)` gives the 32-byte public key as hex for the enrollment command and for display.

pairs.source_norm: signing_message is jsondumps separators ensure_asciifalseencodeutf8 jsonstringify is not byteidentical to jsondumps in general controlcharacter escaping conventions u2028u2029 handling across jsonjs history and the one that actually differs unpaired utf16 surrogates which of the mandates two options proveandrestrict vs reimplement does the page take
pairs.source_text: `signing._message` is `json.dumps([...], separators=(",",":"), ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")`. `JSON.stringify` is not byte-identical to `json.dumps` in general (control-character escaping conventions, U+2028/U+2029 handling across JSON/JS history, and — the one that actually differs — unpaired UTF-16 surrogates). Which of the mandate's two options (prove-and-restrict vs. reimplement) does the page take?
pairs.target_text: Reimplement: the page does not call `JSON.stringify` for the signed message at all. `pyJsonString`/`pyJsonArray` in `nestor/ui_page.py`'s script hand-encode each string exactly the way CPython's `json.dumps` does for this call's arguments — escape `"`, `\`, and code points below 0x20 (using `\b\t\n\f\r` where Python does, `\u00XX` otherwise), and emit every other code point literally, matching `ensure_ascii=False`. This was verified — not assumed — against live Chromium 1194 and CPython 3.11 side by side, across six cases including a non-ASCII letter, an embedded `\"`, raw control bytes 0x00/0x1f/0x7f, a backslash, and a non-BMP emoji: `pyJsonArray` and `json.dumps(..., separators=(",",":"), ensure_ascii=False)` produced identical strings AND identical UTF-8 bytes (via `TextEncoder`) in every case. The one place the two languages provably cannot agree — an UNPAIRED UTF-16 surrogate in `source_norm`/`target_text`/`verifier`, which Python's `str.encode("utf-8")` refuses outright (`UnicodeEncodeError`, no `surrogatepass`) but `TextEncoder` silently replaces with U+FFFD — is detected client-side (`hasLoneSurrogate`) and refused with a clear message BEFORE any bytes are built or signed, rather than silently producing bytes Python could never have produced from the same string.
